content: Individuals undergoing hemodialysis, those living with hepatitis C virus (HCV) or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infections, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and men who have sex with men are identified as populations at higher risk for hepatitis D virus (HDV) infection. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued a conditional recommendation for testing in these groups, although the evidence supporting this recommendation is of very low certainty. The 2024 WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of testing and case-finding for HDV infection. WHO acknowledges the rapidly evolving landscape of HDV treatment. Historically, pegylated interferon-alpha (PEG-IFNα) was the only available treatment for chronic hepatitis D (CHD), but it was associated with poor efficacy, significant side effects, and numerous contraindications. WHO continues to monitor the outcomes of ongoing HDV treatment trials and plans to issue formal treatment recommendations as more evidence becomes available. HDV is a small, defective RNA virus that requires hepatitis B virus (HBV) for its replication, packaging, secretion, and entry into host cells. Consequently, HDV can only infect individuals who are also infected with HBV. There are eight genotypes of HDV, with genotype 1 being the most prevalent globally. Other genotypes are regionally distributed, such as genotype 2 in Asia, genotype 3 in South America, genotype 4 in Eastern Asia, genotype 5 in Western Africa, and genotypes 6 to 8 in Central Africa. There are two primary types of HDV infection: coinfection and superinfection. Coinfection occurs when an individual is simultaneously infected with HBV and HDV, leading to an increased risk of severe acute hepatitis and acute liver failure. Recovery from coinfection is typically complete, and chronic infection is rare. Superinfection, on the other hand, occurs in individuals with pre-existing chronic HBV infection (CHB) and often progresses to chronic hepatitis D (CHD). This condition is associated with a higher risk of rapid progression to liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). CHD is considered the most aggressive form of viral hepatitis due to its accelerated progression to severe liver disease compared to CHB alone. Globally, HDV infection is estimated to contribute to one in six cases of cirrhosis and one in five cases of liver cancer among individuals with CHB. A large study in France involving 1,112 individuals with HDV found that after three years of follow-up, 49% had cirrhosis, 24% experienced liver decompensation, 9% developed HCC, and 5% had died, with liver-related mortality accounting for 71% of deaths. The natural history of CHD is not well understood, but longitudinal studies have identified factors associated with disease progression, including male sex, older age, concurrent HIV or HCV infection, persistent HDV viremia, active HBV replication, diabetes, and obesity. HDV shares transmission routes with HBV, including exposure to infected blood and body fluids (e.g., semen, saliva), injection drug use with shared needles, sexual contact with an infected partner, needle-stick injuries, transfusion of contaminated blood products, and sharing personal items like razors. Mother-to-child transmission of HDV is rare. The prevalence of HDV infection varies geographically, with endemic regions including Mongolia, the Republic of Moldova, parts of Western and Central Africa, Central Asia, Eastern Europe, some Pacific Islands, and the Amazon Basin. Factors influencing this distribution include migration, socioeconomic conditions, HBV vaccination coverage, and differences in HDV genotypes. Testing for HDV infection involves serological methods to detect exposure (past or current infection) and molecular techniques to confirm active infection. Serological markers include hepatitis D antigen and anti-HDV antibodies (IgM, IgG, or total). Anti-HDV antibodies are the most commonly used markers for screening. Molecular testing, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), is used to detect HDV RNA and quantify viral load, which is essential for monitoring treatment response. Challenges in diagnosing HDV include low rates of antibody testing, even in high-income settings, and suboptimal performance of HDV RNA assays, particularly for African genotypes 5 to 8. Standardized testing approaches and algorithms for HDV diagnosis are lacking. Until recently, PEG-IFNα was the only treatment option for CHD, but it had limited efficacy, significant side effects, and frequent relapses. Approximately 30% of treated individuals achieved undetectable HDV RNA levels 24 weeks after treatment, but relapses were common. Nucleoside analogues used for HBV treatment have shown no benefit in controlling HDV. However, the HDV treatment landscape is rapidly evolving, with novel agents demonstrating promising results in clinical trials. In 2023, bulevirtide received approval from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for treating CHD in adults with detectable HDV RNA and compensated liver disease. Clinical trials have shown that bulevirtide, administered as monotherapy or in combination with PEG-IFNα, significantly reduces HDV RNA levels. The treatment is well-tolerated, with no reports of serious drug-related adverse events. WHO recommends two main approaches for HDV testing: universal anti-HDV antibody testing for all individuals with CHB (HBsAg-positive) and focused testing for high-risk groups. Universal testing involves routine anti-HDV antibody testing for all HBsAg-positive individuals, regardless of risk factors. Focused testing targets specific populations at increased risk of HDV infection, such as individuals from endemic regions, people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, sex workers, individuals with HIV or HCV, hemodialysis recipients, and those with advanced liver disease. Evidence for the impact and cost-effectiveness of these testing approaches is limited. Studies have shown low uptake of HDV testing in high-income settings, with many individuals with CHD remaining undiagnosed. Universal testing strategies, such as laboratory-based reflex testing, have been associated with increased case detection rates. The WHO Guidelines Development Group recognizes the need to expand HDV testing to address the current low uptake and improve case detection. Identifying individuals with HDV infection is crucial for implementing preventive interventions, linking patients to counseling and treatment, and enhancing monitoring for early detection of liver cancer. Expanded testing would also improve the availability of high-quality epidemiological data to better understand the national and global burden of HDV infection.
